name: Narthana Vallabeswarar Temple, Thirukoodalaiyatrur
deity: Shiva as Narthana Vallabeswarar (Nerikattunayakar), with the goddesses Gnanasakthi and Parasakthi
period: A Paadal Petra Sthalam of Nadu Nadu at the meeting of the Vellar and the Manimuktha, sung by Sundarar in the Tevaram (8th century)
dynasty: Chola foundation, rebuilt in the Nayak period
summary: Where the Vellar and the Manimuktha meet, Shiva is worshipped as Narthana Vallabeswarar and as Nerikattunayakar, the Lord who walked out to show Sundarar the road he had missed.

sections.history: Thirukoodalaiyatrur is a village of Cuddalore district lying west of Chidambaram, between Srimushnam and Sethiyathope, and its name tells its setting: koodal, the meeting, of two rivers. Here the Manimuktha flows into the Vellar, and devotees call the place Dakshina Prayagai, the Prayag of the south. The temple is one of the 276 Paadal Petra Sthalams and is counted among the shrines of Nadu Nadu, praised in a single pathigam of Sundarar. The first shrine is believed to go back to the Cholas, while much of the present stone fabric is the work of the Nayak period, around the sixteenth century.
sections.architecture: The temple is a walled village shrine of the river country, built in the Dravidian manner, with the sanctum of the lingam facing a mandapa and Nandi. An unusual feature is that the goddess has two shrines of her own, one for Gnanasakthi and one for Parasakthi. Besides the rivers, the temple counts the Brahma, Agastya and Katyayana theerthams as its sacred waters, and on the first three days of Panguni the morning sun reaches in to touch the lingam.
sections.legends: The sthala purana belongs to Sundarar. Travelling towards Thirumuthukundram, today's Vriddhachalam, the saint passed this village without stopping to worship. On the road an aged Brahmin fell in with him and, when Sundarar asked the way, led him on before vanishing. Only then did Sundarar understand that Shiva himself had walked beside him, and he sang his pathigam in wonder that the Lord of Koodalaiyatrur had come along that road. So the Lord is also called Nerikattunayakar, the guide who shows the path.
sections.festivals: The chief festival is the brahmotsavam held around Masi Magam in February–March, among the four annual festivals of the temple. In the first days of Panguni devotees gather to see the sun's rays fall on the lingam. Maha Shivaratri and the monthly Pradosham are also kept; confirm dates locally.
sections.experience: This is a quiet temple of open fields and river sand, best visited unhurriedly. Walk down towards the confluence that gives the village its name, worship the Lord who guided a wandering saint, and visit both shrines of the goddess. Pilgrims often pair it with Vriddhachalam, the destination of Sundarar's journey, and with the temples around Chidambaram.

visit.timings: Open daily in morning and evening sessions with a midday closure, as at most village temples of the region. Confirm current timings locally before visiting.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional dress is expected — shoulders and knees covered; footwear is left outside before entering. Follow the posted rules and the priests' guidance.
visit.photography: Photography is not permitted inside the sanctum; in the outer areas, ask the temple staff before taking pictures, especially of rituals.
visit.gettingThere: Thirukoodalaiyatrur lies some 25 km west of Chidambaram, a short drive from Sethiyathope on the way towards Srimushnam; local buses and hired cars serve the village. Chidambaram is the nearest convenient railway station, with Vriddhachalam Junction also within reach; Puducherry and Tiruchirappalli are the nearest airports.
